ticket.title: Shared target-dir plus sccache stall on the build lock under concurrent repos and long-lived MCP servers
ticket.description:
DECISION 2026-10-30 (owner): the shared target directory STAYS. Rationale recorded: it is worth the serialisation. The remaining work is therefore not to un-share it but to make the stall legible - `Blocking waiting for file lock on build directory` names neither the repository nor the process holding it.

Measured symptoms this session, macOS 12.7.6, cargo/rustc 1.99.1, sccache 0.18.0: four stalls. Two distinct causes, both this repository own processes: (1) a cargo orphaned by a killed command still holding target/debug/.cargo-lock with its cwd in a member repo - found with lsof on the lock file; (2) an sccache deadlock, two rustc --crate-name ring at 0% CPU, one orphaned from an already-finished build. Killing the orphan released both. The remedy and the isolated-target escape hatch are in CONTRIBUTING.md, including the caveat that CARGO_TARGET_DIR breaks miter sandbox tests.
acceptance_criteria:
PROPOSAL 2026-11-07, after measuring. Short version: the shared target directory and sccache are both fine and should stay. The multi-minute builds were not the lock - they were sccache being switched off, by me, on every command.

WHAT THE CONFIG ALREADY DOES, correctly:
  [build] target-dir = "target"      one build graph for all eleven repositories
  [build] rustc-wrapper = "sccache"  compiler cache, 15 GiB, currently 12 GiB warm
  [build] incremental = false        deliberate; sccache covers the same ground without the disk growth (GB-187)

THE MEASUREMENT THAT CHANGES THE DIAGNOSIS:
  sccache --show-stats -> 6 compile requests, 0 executed, 0 hits, 0 misses
  sccache --zero-stats; cargo check -p gaugeblock-contracts (wrapper left enabled)
      -> 27 requests, 23 executed, 21 hits, 1 miss   = 91 percent hit rate on a warm cache
So the cache holds exactly what it is meant to hold. It served nothing because every build in this session ran with `RUSTC_WRAPPER=` in front of it, which is the documented workaround for the GB-259 stall. A workaround for an intermittent hang had become the default posture, and the cost of that posture was every build in this session: 5m, 7m, 8m, 17m and 18m for three-line diffs.

WHAT TO DO, in order of payoff, none of which drops the shared directory or the cache:

1. STOP DISABLING THE WRAPPER BY DEFAULT. Remove `RUSTC_WRAPPER=` from the working habits and from any script that carries it. If a specific invocation hits the GB-259 stall, bypass for that invocation only and say so in the output.

2. WATCHDOG INSTEAD OF BYPASS. The stall's signature is a build that produces no output for minutes while rustc is idle. A wrapper script that samples output and, after N idle minutes, kills the build, prints `sccache --show-stats` and re-runs once with the cache bypassed turns an intermittent infinite hang into a documented one-shot cost. That is strictly better than pre-emptively disabling the cache for every build to avoid a rare failure.

3. MAKE LOCK WAITING VISIBLE, DO NOT FIGHT IT. Cargo serialises writers on one target directory by design; two concurrent builds on the shared target cannot both hold it, and no configuration changes that. What can change is whether the waiting is visible: a thin wrapper that takes an exclusive lock, prints who holds it and roughly how long, and then proceeds, converts an unexplained eight-minute silence into 'queued behind benchwork, started 4m ago'. The measured cost this session was dominated by exactly this waiting, because I launched two and three builds in parallel from different repositories that share one target.

4. SPILL FOR DELIBERATE PARALLELISM. When two builds genuinely must overlap - an MCP server rebuild while a gate runs, say - give the second one `CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target/.spill/<name>`. It stays under the shared root, it is cheap because sccache serves the dependencies, and it can be pruned with one command. This is the only option here that changes behaviour rather than visibility, and it should be opt-in rather than automatic: a spill directory that nobody prunes is how the 23 GB target became a disk failure.

5. RECORD THE HIT RATE. A one-line `sccache --show-stats` summary at the end of a suite-level build, or in the gate output, makes the next regression in cache effectiveness visible immediately. Today's 91 percent is a number worth keeping; a drop to 20 percent would mean the wrapper is being bypassed again, and nothing else in the suite would notice.

WHAT I AM NOT PROPOSING: removing the shared target directory, removing sccache, or switching to sccache-only with per-build target dirs. All three trade a real benefit for a problem that the measurements show is mostly self-inflicted.

HONEST LIMIT: none of this makes concurrent builds on one machine faster than serial builds. It makes the serialisation visible and stops paying a compile-everything tax to avoid a hang that has a repro and a one-shot workaround. If parallel throughput is the actual goal, the answer is more machines, not more configuration.

RUSTC_WRAPPER= for the affected crate, costing one cold dependency compile).

events.description: Measured on macOS 12.7.6 (x86_64), cargo/rustc 1.99.1, sccache 0.18.0, during the GB-130/GB-234 session. Symptom: a gate command prints "Blocking waiting for file lock on build directory" and never advances, or reaches a crate name and stops at 0% CPU; the wrapping shell then hits its own timeout and kills the process group, leaving the lock held by an orphan. Observed four times in one session. Two distinct causes were separated: (1) lock contention, where a killed-but-alive cargo from an earlier timed-out command held target/debug/.cargo-lock with cwd in a member repo - confirmed with lsof on the lock file; (2) an sccache deadlock, where two rustc invocations for ring v0.17.14 sat at 0% CPU, one of them orphaned from an already-finished build - killing the orphan released both.

acceptance_criteria: Root CONTRIBUTING.md documents the contention and the remedies, because .cargo/config.toml is the cause
Decide whether build.target-dir stays shared across 11 repositories: it saves disk and cold-build time but serialises them, and any long-lived miter MCP daemon that invokes cargo contends too
Make the stall self-diagnosable - Blocking waiting for file lock gives no hint which repository or daemon holds it
